name: Rafael Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead rail-crossing signal software at a tech company, where I am among the best at tracing a false alarm. I use AI occasionally to understand old code, but check against engineer logs. Elise teaches pottery, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us rent with twelve months of expenses saved and many nearby software firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the rail-signal team that a little AI help can sort repeated faults, but a crossing light still needs a real test. I sometimes use AI to explain old code and compare the answer with the signal log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this software team at a tech company; I am one of the best here at tracing a false warning. Elise teaches pottery classes, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us rent with twelve months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one crossing alarm against the signal log each Wednesday with the rail engineer. We would put 230 monthly into our cash reserve while both incomes hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about work and rent. A green light on a screen cannot stop a train at a broken crossing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fault did you find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A warning stayed green in our test after the crossing sensor lost power. I checked the engineer’s log before the software update was sent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI only sometimes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me understand a tangled old function. The signal log and the engineer’s test decide whether the code is right.

say: I want **crossing alarms** checked against engineer logs.
I use **AI occasionally** for code explanations, then verify them.
think: I have **twelve months saved** from higher lead pay and Elise’s pottery classes.
I see **rent covered** with our current wages and twelve-month reserve.
do: **Check crossing alarms** with rail engineer each Wednesday.
**Save 230 monthly** in cash reserve while both incomes hold.
S0.quote: A green light on a screen cannot stop a train at a broken crossing.
fieldNote: His **lead skill** is tracing false signal warnings, without claiming field certification.
A **year of savings** supports current rent while both adults work and their grown children live independently.

steps.text: Check one crossing alarm with rail engineer each Wednesday
Save 230 monthly while developer pay and pottery income continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, planning and coding could reduce our signal software team. I would want the workers and rail engineer to know who signs a crossing change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one reviewer checks several automated lines. Twelve months saved gives us time, but Elise’s pottery classes cannot replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for written lead hours and approval for two paid hours each week to learn the AI fault checker on simulated crossings. If approved, I’d test one power-loss fault with engineer sign-off and keep checking a real fault log each Wednesday; I would stay in the developer role while management decides the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours but willing to test the tool safely. A timetable does not know the smell of a hot signal box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you simulate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut power to a fake crossing sensor and see whether the checker marks the alarm unsafe. The rail engineer would sign off the test before any live trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing real faults and wait for written staffing numbers. I would not put a new checker on live crossings without approval.

say: I want **written lead hours** before automated signal checks change the team.
I want **engineer sign-off** before any checker affects a live crossing.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** if one reviewer covers several automated rail lines.
I have **twelve months saved**, but a lost developer wage would still matter.
do: **Learn AI fault checker** weekly only with approved paid time, simulated faults and engineer sign-off.
**Keep checking real faults** each Wednesday while developer role remains paid.
S1.quote: A timetable does not know the smell of a hot signal box.
fieldNote: He requests **new paid AI learning** on fake power failures and retains engineer control of live releases.
His **current fault checks** continue while management decides staffing, without assuming another job exists.

steps.text: Practise AI fault checker weekly only with approved paid time and simulated engineer-reviewed crossings
Keep checking real crossing faults each Wednesday while lead role pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write signal code and diagnose logs cheaper than our team. Robots repairing track equipment may follow around 2031, after the desk work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer role could end even though I know the crossings well. Twelve months saved lets us search, but Elise’s classes do not pay the whole rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written notice of any lead cuts and keep a copy of three verified crossing failures I can explain to another employer. If my job ends after 2028, I’d search qualified paid local rail-control vacancies only where wages cover rent and bills; I would keep the twelve-month reserve for household costs instead of buying track tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about a lost wage, even with savings. A signal log is evidence of work, not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would rail-control work survive AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. I would take only a real paid opening and keep looking if it shrank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a control job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local rail operators and software firms first. Elise’s pottery classes and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach signal code first.
I expect **track robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end.
I know **twelve months saved** buys search time, not pay.
do: **Record three crossing failures** and request written lead-cut notice while current job pays.
**Search rail-control vacancies** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A signal log is evidence of work, not a job offer.
fieldNote: His **verified fault examples** make current safety work legible to another employer without claiming field certification.
The **local search** starts after job loss and requires qualification, a real paid vacancy and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Record three verified crossing failures while developer role pays
Search qualified paid local rail-control vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn how a failed crossing is reported on site before code changes. Robots repairing tracks may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the longer warning to learn rail-signal safety rules while I still earn a developer wage. A theory course would not qualify me to sign a live track release, and I would keep ten months of expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d enrol in an available rail-signal safety theory course only if its fee is at most 180 and at least ten months of expenses stay saved. I’d practise one simulated fault log weekly with the instructor and save 210 monthly while both incomes hold; I would take no live signal duty without funded paid supervised assessment and current qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role, but a bounded course lets me learn the safety rules without touching a live signal. A failed crossing is a place with people waiting, not just an error message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the instructor check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The instructor would check my fault entry, safe-stop order and clearance record on a simulated log. I would not sign a live track release from a theory lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the operator cannot fund training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait or ask a hiring rail operator whether it funds a course tied to a paid vacancy. I would not dip below our ten-month reserve on speculation.

say: I want **signal-safety theory** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **track robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can study **rail-signal rules** while my developer wage continues.
I need **ten months untouched** after any course fee and current qualification before live duty.
do: **Enrol in safety theory** only if available, fee at most 180 and ten-month reserve remains.
**Practise simulated fault logs** weekly with instructor; save 210 monthly while both incomes hold.
Take **no live signal duty** without funded paid supervised assessment and current qualification.
feel: **Anxious but measured** with a bounded safety course.
S3.quote: A failed crossing is a place with people waiting, not just an error message.
fieldNote: His **self-funded course** has an explicit fee cap and reserve floor, and uses simulated rather than live faults.
Theory **does not qualify him** for track release; live duty still needs funded paid supervision and certification.

steps.text: Enrol in signal theory, practise logs only if available, fee at most 180, ten-month reserve intact
Save 210 monthly while developer pay and pottery income continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives rail operators time to set human safety rules and families time to check their income. Robots repairing physical track equipment may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Twelve months saved keeps the next few years secure, but I cannot assume a signal-room vacancy later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing crossing faults and save 220 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate; if my developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local signal-operations vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about work later but secure in the next few years. I can check a real crossing today, even if I cannot name the job I will have in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the developer job to train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would take paid supervised training only while my current wage remains or after a written paid offer. I would not resign for an unfunded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and Elise and I will plan from wages and verified figures.

I expect **track robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I see **current bills secure** with twelve months saved.
do: Keep reviewing crossings; take **paid supervised training** only while current wage remains or after written paid offer.

fieldNote: He ties **retirement timing** to verified figures rather than a birthday.
The **year of savings** supports near-term security without assuming children’s wages or a future rail post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before a qualified paid local rail-control opening exists. Written notice and a real bill-covering vacancy would help us use savings deliberately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would work on a live crossing without a safety qualification. I would not sign a track release until a qualified engineer trained and checked me.

headlineQuote: I would not sign a track release until a qualified engineer trained and checked me.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, higher pay and twelve months saved.
He and Elise **rent** while their grown children live separately.
He **uses AI occasionally** but checks crossing alarms against engineer logs.
He considers **signal-room work** only with paid approval, funded safety training and qualified supervision.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before qualified paid local rail work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a real bill-covering local rail-control vacancy would help.
